note: Automating exemplar construction removes a hidden human dependency, which is worth tracing when an audit asks who authored a prompt.
title: Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models

reading.body:
Automatic prompt construction matched or beat hand-written examples on ten public reasoning benchmarks, which means the human labor in chain-of-thought prompting is optional rather than load-bearing.

The pattern is narrow but clean. Manual chain-of-thought prompting works by supplying the model with worked examples, and those examples have historically been written by people who understand the task. Auto-CoT has the model generate the reasoning chains itself, and adds diversity in question selection because generated chains can be wrong. Across ten public reasoning tests with GPT-3, the automatic demonstrations performed as well as or better than the manual ones. The human contribution to the prompt was not what made the prompt work.

For AI systems specifically, this shifts where effort and cost sit. Prompt engineering has been treated as skilled, task-specific labor, and this result says a large part of it can be generated. It also changes the audit question. If a model writes its own examples, then asking who authored a prompt has a different answer than it did before, and the note attached to this paper flags exactly that. Generated examples can contain errors, so the removal of a human writer is not the same as the removal of a human check.

What the data does not cover is scale or cost. Ten public benchmarks and one model family, GPT-3, are the entire evidence base here, and the paper is a 2022 preprint with 1,042 citations. Nothing in it speaks to compute, data centers, or power, and it should not be read as a claim about them. The result is about who writes the examples, not about how much hardware runs them.

explain_beginner: The paper looks at a way to help large language models solve reasoning problems by showing them example solutions. Normally, people must write those examples by hand, which takes time and task-specific effort. The authors tested letting the model create the examples itself, using a simple instruction to reason in steps. Because model-written examples can contain errors, they added variety when choosing questions. Their method, Auto-CoT, matched or beat the human-written example approach on ten public reasoning tests with GPT-3. This matters because it can reduce manual work and make prompting easier to reuse.
explain_business: This research suggests companies can reduce human effort when using large language models for reasoning tasks. Instead of paying experts to write example solutions for each task, teams can let the model generate examples automatically. The method, Auto-CoT, selects varied questions and creates reasoning steps, then uses them as prompts. On ten public reasoning tests with GPT-3, it performed as well as or better than manually designed examples. For executives, this informs decisions about reducing manual prompt design, lowering prompt engineering costs, and auditing who or what authored prompts, while noting generated examples may contain mistakes.
explain_practitioner: The paper addresses CoT prompting, where demonstrations include a question and reasoning chain. Manual demonstrations perform well but require hand-crafted task-specific examples. The authors propose Auto-CoT. It uses an LLM with a simple step-by-step prompt to generate reasoning chains for demonstrations one by one. Since generated chains can be wrong, Auto-CoT samples questions for diversity before generating chains. On ten public benchmark reasoning tasks with GPT-3, Auto-CoT consistently matched or exceeded manual CoT. The key result is that automatic demonstration construction can remove the need for manual, task-specific demonstration design while preserving or improving performance.
